meta.blurb: Hazel Quinn comes to Maple Street for one month to fix a baker's books. Jonas Reed is grumpy, proud and up at three every morning. Can a cheerful stranger save his bakery, and can he save her heart?
meta.bible: Hazel Quinn: a kind, cheerful bookkeeper of twenty-nine from the city, good with numbers, bad with ovens. Jonas Reed: the Baker of Reed's Bakery, thirty-four, grumpy, proud, tall, up at three every morning; he has one rule, no talking before the first bread. Ada Reed: Jonas's younger sister, who runs the flower shop across the street and hires Hazel. Walter Reed: Jonas's late father, who started the bakery and died two years ago. Old Margaret: the forty-year-old sourdough Starter that Walter began; nobody touches it but Jonas. Mrs Pell: an eighty-year-old neighbour and the first customer every morning. Mr Ferris: the landlord of the building, fair but busy. Ms Vance: the manager of Golden Crust, a chain bakery that opens across the street. Mr Bello: the plumber, who fixes things for friends. Biscuit: the grey bakery cat. Ashby Green: a small town. Maple Street: its main street. The Autumn Festival: the bread contest in six weeks. Reed's Bakery: Maple Street, with a blue door and a bell. The Rye loaf: Walter's dark rye, which Jonas has not baked since he died. Sourdough, Starter, Dough, Oven, Flour, Loaf, Loaves, Rye, Cinnamon, Subscription, Lease, Rent, Bookkeeper, Festival, Market, Counter, Shoebox, Notebook. Voice and tone: warm, funny and gentle, a slow-burn love story between a sunny person and a grumpy one; real ending with a kiss and a shared future; no cruelty.

A1A2: Hazel Quinn got off the bus in a small town at dawn.
Ada gave Hazel a key and said, “My brother needs help.”
Jonas Reed was tall, tired and covered in white flour.
“I don't need help,” said Jonas. “I need a new oven.”
On the wall was a card with three strange rules.
Hazel slept above the flower shop and woke at three.
The bakery's papers were all inside one old shoebox.
Jonas gave Mrs Pell a bag of bread and took no money.
Hazel said, “You lose money every month.” Jonas did not answer.
Mr Ferris owned the building and he came to see Jonas.
Mr Ferris gave Jonas six weeks to show that the bakery could stay.
Hazel asked to work at the counter and learn the shop.
Hazel dropped a loaf, but the customers still smiled.
Hazel wrote a card for the rolls and they sold quickly.
Walter Reed started the bakery forty years ago.
Hazel asked about the rye bread, and Jonas walked away.
At three in the morning Hazel came down to the kitchen.
Jonas showed Hazel the jar and said, “This is Old Margaret.”
Jonas told Hazel why he came back home to bake.
Hazel had an idea about a market stall and a bread plan.
Jonas said no, but his sister Ada said, “Try it once.”
On Saturday it rained, but people still came for bread.
Mrs Pell told Hazel, “Jonas used to laugh a lot.”
All the bread was sold, and Jonas laughed out loud.
A big gold sign went up across the street.
Hazel said, “We cannot be cheaper. We can be better.”
Hazel called the library, the school and the inn.
Ten children came to bake bread and made a big mess.
Jonas was kind to a small boy and showed him how.
A letter came for Hazel, and it offered her a job.
Golden Crust opened, and nobody came to Reed's.
Jonas said, “Maybe Mr Ferris should give the shop away.”
On Thursday night the big oven stopped working.
The school said Jonas could use its big kitchen.
Hazel and Jonas baked until morning and nearly kissed.
Jonas found the letter and learned about the city job.
They argued, and Jonas said, “People always leave.”
Hazel packed her bag, and Ada was angry with them both.
Mrs Pell gave Jonas an old notebook that was his father's.
Jonas baked his father's rye bread for the first time.
Hazel went to the bus stop but she did not get on.
On festival day the whole town came to the bread contest.
Jonas found Hazel and said, “I am sorry.” She smiled.
Mr Ferris tasted the rye bread and smiled, and everyone cheered.
Mr Ferris gave Jonas the shop for ten more years.
Ms Vance from Golden Crust tried the rye and nodded.
That night Jonas said, “Please stay.” Hazel said, “I will.”
Jonas kissed Hazel, and Biscuit the cat looked away.
In winter the shop sign said Reed and Quinn.
At three in the morning Jonas smiled and said, “Good morning.”
B1B2: Hazel Quinn steps off the early bus with one suitcase and a small, tired smile. Maple Street is still dark, but the air already smells like fresh bread.
Ada Reed runs the flower shop across the street, and she has hired Hazel for one month. She says her brother's bakery is losing money, but he will not look at the numbers.
Jonas Reed is tall and covered in flour, and he looks at Hazel as if she were a mouse in his kitchen. He says only one word, which is “Later,” and goes back to his work.
When the first loaves are out, Jonas finally agrees to speak to her. He says that he does not need a bookkeeper, because he only needs a better oven.
On the kitchen wall hangs a card with three rules in black pen. The first one says that nobody may talk before the first bread comes out of the oven.
Hazel's new room is small, but the bed is soft and the window looks at the bakery. At three in the morning a yellow light comes on across the street, and she knows that Jonas is already working.
Jonas keeps every receipt, bill and letter in a battered shoebox, and none of them are in order. Hazel sits down with a pencil and a cup of tea and begins to sort them.
Hazel notices that Jonas gives away a lot of bread. Mrs Pell, the school and the church all go home with free loaves, and he never writes it down.
That evening Hazel shows Jonas her neat columns of numbers. He looks at them for a long time and then says that bread is not a number.
Mr Ferris, who owns the building, calls in with bad news. A big bakery company called Golden Crust has asked to rent the shop, and it can pay a much higher rent.
Mr Ferris says he will decide the day after the Autumn Festival, which is six weeks away. If the bakery can pay a fair rent by then, Jonas can stay.
Hazel decides that numbers alone will not save the bakery, so she asks to work at the counter. Jonas says she will be terrible at it, but he gives her an apron.
Hazel is clumsy at the counter. She drops a loaf, gets the change wrong twice and forgets the names of the breads, but the customers like her at once.
On the fifth day Hazel writes little cards to tell customers what each bread is. The cinnamon rolls sell out before ten o'clock for the first time in months.
A photo on the wall shows an older man with Jonas's grey eyes. Ada says it is their father Walter, who began the bakery and its sourdough starter, which they call Old Margaret.
Hazel asks Jonas why the shop never sells the dark rye that is written on the old sign. His face closes like a door, and he walks out into the yard without a word.
Hazel cannot sleep, so at three in the morning she crosses the street and knocks. Jonas lets her in, gives her an apron and shows her how to fold the dough.
Jonas lifts the lid from a big jar of bubbling dough. He says it is Old Margaret, the starter, and that it is older than he is.
As the sky turns grey, Jonas tells Hazel that he once worked in a fine city restaurant. When his father became ill he came home, and he has never been able to leave again.
Hazel has an idea. The bakery could sell at the Saturday market and let neighbours pay each month for a loaf every week.
Jonas says no at first, because he does not like crowds or change. Ada stands in front of him with her hands on her hips until he agrees to try one Saturday.
Saturday is cold and wet, and Jonas stands under the awning with a dark face. Hazel holds up a bright sign that says Warm Bread, and soon there is a line down the street.
Mrs Pell takes Hazel's arm and says that when Jonas was a boy he was the funniest child in town. He stopped laughing, she says, on the day his father died.
By two o'clock every loaf has gone. When Hazel pours out the coins and starts to count, Jonas laughs out loud for the first time since she met him.
On Monday workmen hang a bright gold sign across the street. It says Golden Crust, Opening Soon, and Jonas sees it first.
Jonas is angry and says the town will leave him for cheap bread. Hazel stays calm and says they cannot win by being cheaper, only by being exactly what the big shop can never be.
Hazel spends two days on the phone. By Friday the library café, the school and the village inn have all agreed to buy bread from Reed's every week.
Hazel organises a baking class for ten children. Flour flies through the air, dough sticks to the ceiling, and the kitchen has never been so noisy.
A small boy is afraid he will ruin his bread, and Jonas kneels beside him. He guides the boy's hands slowly and quietly, and Hazel feels her heart turn over.
A letter arrives from Hazel's old boss in the city. It offers her a good job from January, and she puts it in her bag and tells no one.
The new shop opens with free coffee, music and very cheap bread. For three days, hardly anyone comes through the blue door of Reed's.
On the third night Jonas sits alone in the dark kitchen. He tells Hazel that maybe Mr Ferris should rent the shop to someone who is better at all this.
On Thursday night the big oven makes a loud bang and goes cold. Mr Bello, the plumber, looks inside and says it will take a week to repair.
The head teacher offers the big school kitchen, and neighbours carry trays of dough there through the dark. Mrs Pell brings a thermos of tea, and Ada brings lanterns.
They bake side by side until morning, tired and covered in flour. For a moment they stand very close, but the school caretaker walks in with his keys.
Hazel's bag tips over, and the city letter slides across the floor. Jonas picks it up, reads it and goes cold, and his old frown returns.
Hazel says that she was going to tell him. Jonas says that people always leave, and she answers that he pushes people away before they can.
That night Hazel packs her suitcase in the little room. Ada comes in, folds her arms and says that her brother and her friend are both being fools.
Mrs Pell visits Jonas with a worn little notebook. It belonged to his father, and on the last page Walter has written a few lines for his son.
Jonas reads the page again and again, and then he begins to bake. He makes his father's dark rye for the first time since Walter died, and he cries a little as the dough rises.
At the bus stop Hazel watches the bus come and go without her. She turns her suitcase around, rings her old boss, and says a polite no.
The Autumn Festival arrives with flags, music and a long table of bread from all over the county. Golden Crust has entered too, with shiny, perfect loaves.
Jonas finds Hazel in the crowd and holds out a warm loaf. He says he was wrong and afraid, and that she is the best thing that has happened to the bakery.
Mr Ferris tastes the dark rye and closes his eyes. The crowd cheers, and Hazel shows him new numbers that prove the bakery can pay its rent.
Mr Ferris says Golden Crust offered more money, but he would rather keep the town's bakery. He gives Jonas a ten-year lease at a fair rent.
Ms Vance, the manager of Golden Crust, tastes the rye and nods slowly. She tells Jonas that it is the best bread she has ever eaten, and that she will not forget it.
After the festival, they sit on the bakery step in the evening light. Jonas asks her to stay, and Hazel tells him she has wanted to ever since the rainy Saturday.
Jonas takes her floury hand and kisses her at last. Biscuit the cat, who is watching from the counter, yawns and turns his back.
By winter the bakery has a new sign. It says Reed and Quinn, and Hazel keeps the books while Jonas smiles at customers, a little.
At three in the morning Hazel brings Jonas a coffee, and the oven glows warm. Before the first bread is out, Jonas breaks his own rule and says good morning with a smile.
C1C2: The first bus of the day left Hazel Quinn on the edge of Ashby Green with one suitcase, a handful of coins and a stubborn hope. Maple Street lay quiet and half asleep under the last of the stars. Somewhere ahead of her, the warm smell of baking bread was drifting through the cold air like a promise.

Ada Reed, a small woman with soil under her fingernails, welcomed Hazel into her flower shop and pressed a key into her hand. She explained that her older brother owned the bakery across the street and that it had been losing money for two years without his noticing. Hazel had lost her office job in the city only a week before, so the offer of one month's work felt like a gift.

Behind the counter of Reed's Bakery stood a tall man with flour up to his elbows and a frown that looked as if it had been there for years. He gave Hazel one long look, said a single word, which was “Later,” and turned back to his work. It was not the warm welcome she had hoped for, but the bread on the shelves was so beautiful that she forgave him at once.

Only when the first loaves were cooling on the racks did Jonas agree to speak to her, and then he kept it short. He told her that he did not need a bookkeeper, that Ada should not have asked, and that what the bakery really wanted was a new oven. Hazel, who had been told no by far fiercer people than a baker, simply asked where he kept the paperwork.

A card in square black handwriting hung beside the oven, and Hazel read it twice to be sure she had understood. There was to be no talking before the first bread came out, no touching the starter without permission, and no cutting a loaf with the wrong knife. She decided, on the spot, that anyone who took bread this seriously could not be as cold as he seemed.

Her little room above the flower shop smelled of roses and old wood, and the bed was softer than any she had slept in for months. At three in the morning, however, a square of yellow light flickered on in the window across the street, and the faint, steady thump of kneading drifted over the cobbles. Hazel lay still and listened, wondering what sort of man begins his day when the rest of the town is dreaming.

The accounts of Reed's Bakery turned out to live in a single battered shoebox, along with a pencil stub, two buttons and a very old biscuit. Hazel tipped everything onto the table, rolled up her sleeves and began sorting, one slip of paper at a time. By evening she had found three unpaid bills, one lost cheque and a drawer of letters that nobody had dared to open.

As Hazel watched the morning rush, she noticed that a good part of the bread left the shop without any money coming back. Mrs Pell took her loaf for nothing, the school received a basket every Friday, and the church had its bread free for the Sunday meal. Jonas never wrote any of it down, and he scowled if anyone thanked him.

That evening she laid her tidy columns of figures on the steel table and explained, as gently as she could, that the bakery lost money every single month. Jonas studied the page in silence, his jaw tight, and then muttered that bread was not a number and never would be. Hazel nodded, because he was right, and then she asked him how he planned to pay the rent with it.

Mr Ferris owned the whole row of buildings on Maple Street, and he arrived on Thursday looking apologetic and rather rushed. A chain of bakeries called Golden Crust, he explained, had offered to rent the shop across the road for double the rent, and he had to take such an offer seriously. He was fond of the Reeds, he added, but he was also a man with bills of his own.

Mr Ferris finally agreed to wait until the day after the Autumn Festival, six weeks away, before choosing between the old bakery and the new one. If Jonas could show that his shop paid its way and a fair rent besides, the Reeds could stay. Hazel looked at the calendar, then at the heap of unpaid bills, and understood that her one month had just become the most important month of her life.

Hazel understood, after three days with the shoebox, that numbers alone would never explain why customers came or why they left. She asked Jonas if she could work the counter for a week and learn the shop from the inside. He predicted that she would be terrible at it, tossed her an apron three sizes too large and went back to his dough.

As predicted, Hazel was a disaster behind the counter, for she dropped a loaf, miscounted the change twice and called a seeded plait a pretzel. Yet the customers seemed to enjoy her cheerful honesty, and several of them came back later in the day just to see what she would do next. Jonas watched from the kitchen door with his arms folded, trying very hard not to look interested.

On her fifth day Hazel wrote small cards describing each bread, with a price, a name and one friendly sentence about how it tasted. The cinnamon rolls, which had always been left to cool unnoticed at the back, sold out before ten o'clock for the first time in months. Jonas read the card by the tray, said nothing at all, and quietly started baking twice as many the next morning.

Hazel noticed the photograph above the sink on her eighth morning: an older man with Jonas's grey eyes, laughing with a loaf under each arm. Ada told her, quietly, that it was their father Walter, who had started the bakery forty years ago and had begun the sourdough starter that Jonas still fed every day. They called it Old Margaret, and it was, in a way, the last living piece of him.

Hazel asked an innocent question about the dark rye loaf that was painted on the faded sign above the door. Jonas's face closed like a shutter, and without a word he walked out into the yard and stayed there until the bread was nearly burnt. She did not ask again, but she understood now that the grumpiness was only the outside of something much sadder.

Unable to sleep, Hazel crossed the dark street at three in the morning and knocked softly on the blue door. After a long pause Jonas opened it, looked at her for a moment, and instead of sending her away, tossed her an apron and pushed a bowl of dough across the table. His hands, big and patient, showed her how to fold it, and for once he did not seem to mind the company.

Jonas lifted the lid of a large glass jar, and a sour, sweet smell rose into the warm air. This was Old Margaret, he said in a low voice, the starter his father had begun forty years ago and fed every day of his life. Hazel was only the third person ever allowed to look at it, and she held her breath as if it might wake.

While the first loaves baked, Jonas told her, in short and reluctant sentences, that he used to cook in a fine restaurant in the city. When his father fell ill he had come home for a month, and then two years, and then there had been no one else to take over the ovens. He said it flatly, as though it did not hurt, but his hands kept turning a wooden spoon over and over.

By the third week Hazel had a plan, scribbled on the back of an empty flour sack. The bakery could set up a stall at the Saturday market, and it could offer neighbours a bread subscription, so that they paid each month for a loaf every week. Regular money, she explained, was what turned a lovely shop into a lasting one.

Jonas refused at once, since he disliked crowds, change and being told what to do in his own kitchen. Ada planted herself in front of him with her hands on her hips and said that their father would have tried it, and the argument ended there. He agreed to a single Saturday, and made it clear that he expected to be proved right.

Saturday arrived grey and drenched, and Jonas stood under the dripping awning of the market stall with a face like the weather. Hazel, undaunted, held a hand-painted sign above her head that read Warm Bread, Warm Hello, and before long a line of umbrellas curled down the street. People who had not tasted Reed's loaves in years were suddenly buying two or three at a time.

Between customers, old Mrs Pell took Hazel's arm and confided that Jonas had once been the funniest boy on Maple Street, always doing voices and telling jokes over the counter. He had stopped laughing the day his father died, she said, and had grown a thick shell around himself ever since. She patted Hazel's hand as though she hoped it might be the one to crack it.

By two o'clock the last loaf had been sold, and the table was heavy with damp notes and coins. Hazel poured them out in a shining heap and began to count, and when she announced the total, Jonas threw back his head and laughed. It was a deep, startled sound, as though he had found an old tool in a drawer, and it made her heart do something strange.

On Monday morning a crew of workmen hung a huge gold sign over the empty shop across the street. It read Golden Crust, Opening Soon, in letters so large that Jonas could read them from his own kitchen window. He stood very still for a long time, and the wooden spoon in his hand slowly snapped in two.

Jonas was furious and certain that the whole town would drift away to cheap bread and bright lights. Hazel kept her voice calm and said that they could never win by being cheaper, and that their only chance was to be exactly what a big chain could never be. A bakery that knew your name, she told him, was worth more than a discount.

Hazel spent two days with a telephone pressed to her ear and a list of every business within ten miles. By Friday the library café, the school and the village inn had each agreed to buy bread from Reed's every week, and the numbers in her book were slowly turning from red to black. Jonas baked through the nights to meet the orders, grumbling all the way, but he never once refused.

Hazel's next idea was a Saturday baking class for children, and ten of them arrived in aprons far too big for them. Within minutes flour was drifting through the air like snow, a lump of dough had stuck to the ceiling, and the kitchen had never been so loud. Jonas stood in the middle of it with the look of a man caught in a storm.

One small boy was afraid that he would ruin his loaf, and to Hazel's astonishment Jonas knelt on the floor beside him. He guided the child's hands over the dough with infinite patience, speaking in a voice she had never heard him use. Watching from the doorway, Hazel realised with a little shock that she was in far deeper trouble than any shoebox of bills.

A letter forwarded from the city arrived for Hazel, and the handwriting on the envelope belonged to her old boss. He was opening a new office in January, he wrote, and he wanted her there as head of accounts, with a salary she could hardly have dreamed of a month before. She read it twice, folded it small and tucked it deep into her bag, telling herself that she had plenty of time to decide.

Golden Crust opened on a bright Monday with free coffee, balloons and bread at half the price of Reed's. For three long days the blue door across the street hardly opened at all, and the loaves that Jonas had baked so carefully were left on the shelves. Hazel counted the empty hours and began to fear that being kind and clever might not be enough.

On the third night Hazel found Jonas sitting alone on an upturned crate in the dark, his big hands hanging between his knees. He said, in a voice she did not recognise, that perhaps Mr Ferris should give the building to someone better at all of this. She sat down on the floor facing him and told him firmly that he was the best baker she had ever met and that she was not finished yet.

On Thursday night, just as the weekend orders were due, the old oven gave a loud bang and went cold. Mr Bello the plumber, who had been called out of bed, peered inside with a torch and announced that the repair would take at least a week. A week without bread, Hazel knew, was a week in which the new shop across the road would win the whole town.

Before midnight the news had travelled up and down Maple Street, and the head teacher offered Jonas the use of the school's great kitchen. Neighbours appeared out of the dark carrying trays of dough, Mrs Pell brought a flask of tea, and Ada lit the way with garden lanterns. Jonas had spent two years refusing help from anyone, and now he stood there with a lump in his throat, unable to say a word.

Hazel and Jonas baked side by side until the windows turned pale, passing trays, laughing at nothing and brushing flour from each other's faces. In the quiet before dawn they stood very close, and neither of them moved away, until the caretaker rattled in with his keys and a loud good morning. They sprang apart like guilty teenagers, and Hazel could not stop smiling.

When Hazel's bag tipped over in the bakery that afternoon, the folded letter from the city slid across the floor and stopped at Jonas's boot. He picked it up and read it slowly while she stood frozen, and his face, which had been softening for weeks, set hard again like cooling iron. He handed it back without a word, and the old frown was back where it had always been.

Hazel insisted that she had meant to tell him, and that she had not decided anything yet. Jonas said coldly that people always left in the end, and she answered, more sharply than she intended, that he drove them away before they ever had the chance to stay. The words hung in the warm kitchen, and neither of them could take them back.

That night Hazel folded her clothes into the suitcase with hands that would not stay steady. Ada appeared in the doorway, folded her arms and told her bluntly that she and her brother were both being fools of the first order. Hazel only shook her head, because she could not explain that leaving was the one way she knew to stop her heart from breaking more slowly.

Early the next morning Mrs Pell shuffled into the kitchen and set a worn cloth notebook on the table in front of Jonas. Walter had given it to her for safekeeping, she said, with instructions to hand it over on the day his son needed it most. On the last page, in shaky pencil, he had written that Jonas would bake better than he ever had, if only he stopped being afraid to love things.

Jonas read the last page until the pencil blurred, and then he wiped his eyes with a floury wrist and reached for the rye flour. He followed his father's notes line by line, and the whole kitchen filled with the dark, earthy smell that he had not allowed himself to remember in two years. When the loaves came out, cracked and glossy, he stood holding one in both hands as though it were a living thing.

At the bus stop on the edge of town Hazel watched the morning bus slow, open its doors and, after a long pause, close them again without her. She turned her suitcase around, took out her phone, and told her old boss, politely and clearly, that she would not be taking the job. The strange thing was that she felt no fear at all, only a great light feeling as though she had finally put down something heavy.

The Autumn Festival came at last, with flags strung across the green, a brass band at the corner and a long table laid with bread from every baker in the county. Golden Crust had entered too, with rows of shining, perfectly shaped loaves that looked as though they had come from a factory. The whole of Ashby Green had gathered to taste, and Mr Ferris stood among them with a notebook.

Jonas pushed through the crowd until he found Hazel, and he held out a loaf of rye that was still warm from the oven. He told her, in clumsy and halting words, that he had been wrong and afraid, and that she was the best thing that had ever happened to the bakery and to him. She took the loaf, laughed, and said that for once she was happy to be spoken to before the first bread.

Mr Ferris took a slice of Walter's rye, chewed it slowly with his eyes closed, and murmured that he had not tasted that bread since he was a young man. The crowd, who had been holding its breath, burst into applause, and half the town pressed forward to join Hazel's subscription list on the spot. She handed Mr Ferris a neat folder showing that the bakery now paid its way, with money to spare.

Mr Ferris admitted that Golden Crust had offered him more money, but he declared that a street without its own baker was only a road. He offered Jonas a lease of ten years at a fair rent, on one condition: that the rye loaf returned to the shelves every Saturday. Jonas, who could not speak, shook his hand so hard that the old man winced and laughed.

Ms Vance, the sharp-eyed manager of Golden Crust, took a slice of rye from the table and ate it without a word. She turned to Jonas and told him, with a rueful smile, that it was the best bread she had ever tasted and that her shop could never make it. It was, he thought, a very generous thing to say, and he thanked her honestly.

When the festival had emptied and the lanterns were swaying on their strings, Jonas and Hazel sat side by side on the step of the blue door. He asked, awkwardly and quietly, whether she would stay, and not only for the books. She told him that she had wanted to stay since the rainy Saturday, and probably a good deal longer than that.

Jonas took her floury hand in his, leaned down at last and kissed her, gently and for rather a long time. Biscuit, the grey cat who had ruled the counter for years, watched the whole thing with obvious disapproval, then yawned and turned his back on them. Neither of them noticed, since the entire street seemed to have gone quiet around them.

By the first snow, a painter had climbed a ladder and added a second name to the sign over the blue door, so that it now read Reed and Quinn. Hazel kept the books in a proper ledger at last, the subscriptions grew by the week, and Jonas had even been seen smiling at customers. Mrs Pell remarked that she had not seen the like in thirty years.

At three o'clock on a frosty morning, Hazel crossed the street with two cups of coffee and let herself into the warm, glowing kitchen. Jonas looked up from the dough, and before a single loaf had come out of the oven, he broke the first rule on the wall and said, with a smile, good morning. Behind them, in its jar, Old Margaret bubbled happily, and the day began as every good day on Maple Street should.
